Why this approach? And what breaks under load? Backend interviews ask those follow-ups more than they used to, and this series is about answering them. The ground is data structures and algorithms, complexity in Big-O, and your language's fundamentals, usually in live coding. Backend roles add system and API design, sequel, caching and concurrency.

What has changed is the coding round. Since 2025, it has split in two. Some rounds hand you an assistant and grade how you drive and check it. Canva's does. Meta made one of its two onsite coding rounds a sixty-minute AI-enabled round, and Google is piloting one for reading and debugging code. Others ban assistants. Amazon can disqualify a candidate who uses unapproved AI, Anthropic allows none in interviews unless the interviewer says so, and Google has brought back an in-person round. Underneath is one problem: an assistant can finish a take-home, and nobody sees how. Karat, which sells interviewing services, asked four hundred engineering leaders in its 2026 survey, so read its figures as one vendor's. Seventy-one percent said AI makes technical skills harder to assess. Sixty-two percent of organizations still banned it in technical interviews. So the time has moved to live rounds where the interviewer watches you reason: extending a multi-file project, reading and debugging unfamiliar code, and design discussions with follow-ups. And system design now takes in features that call a large language model, or LLM: streaming, retries, cost measured in tokens, and prompt injection. Ask the recruiter, round by round, whether AI is allowed, and prepare for both. Algorithm practice still matters where it isn't.
